title: A Surrogate Boundary Condition for Improved Accuracy and Performance of Local Modeling in Radiation Transport Simulations
authors: Jonathan Trieloff, Ethan Peterson
abstract: Monte Carlo neutronics analysis of tokamak designs is computationally expensive due to the complex CAD geometries required to accurately model them. Design iteration of port plugs using global transport in the full model is impractical because of the computational cost. To circumvent this, local modeling methods are used. In the local modeling method, a boundary condition is assumed on the port plug, such that particles that leave the port plug do not require transport in the surrounding global model. For this purpose, vacuum and reflective boundaries are assumed, both of which provide poor approximation of the true transport physics in the global model. To improve on current techniques, a surrogate model is presented that provides a physics-informed boundary condition for the component. A neural network is trained to reproduce the boundary condition on the component that represents the behavior of particles returning from the surrounding geometry. Monte Carlo transport is only necessary within the component, and approximate physics from the surrounding region are retained. This approach allows the design in the component to be iterated without requiring full model transport and joining of the component mesh to the global mesh in each iteration. In this work, the surrogate model is evaluated against vacuum and reflective boundaries-- outperforming both in accuracy, with surrogate predictions of the flux in the port plug differing less than 12% from the global transport solution in any given energy bin. The surrogate boundary condition is also demonstrated to be more performant than global transport for the simplified benchmark geometry.

infographic.key_insight: A neural-network surrogate boundary condition improves local neutron transport modeling by approximating particles returning from surrounding geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can iterate tokamak port-plug designs without repeated full-model transport or component-to-global mesh joining.
method: Train a neural network to reproduce the component boundary response from surrounding geometry.
Run Monte Carlo transport only within the component, using the surrogate to approximate returning particles.
Compare local flux predictions with global transport and vacuum or reflective boundary approximations.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a simplified benchmark geometry, surrogate port-plug flux differed by less than 12% from global transport in every energy bin, outperforming vacuum and reflective boundaries in accuracy while running faster than global transport.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and speed gains require validation for realistic tokamak geometries and design changes beyond the demonstrated benchmark.
infographic.paper_title: A Surrogate Boundary Condition for Improved Accuracy and Performance of Local Modeling in Radiation Transport Simulations

title: NeoResearch: Literature- and Experience-Guided Autonomous Time Series Model Discovery
authors: Ze Guo, Mingyue Cheng, Xiaoyu Tao, Shuo Yu, Shangtong Ye
abstract: Developing effective forecasting models for diverse time-series domains requires substantial expert knowledge, evidence from scientific literature on the web, and iterative experimentation. However, translating this knowledge and research experience into model designs requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions. In this paper, we propose NeoResearch, a literature- and experience-guided autonomous research framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as researchers to discover lightweight, domain-specific forecasting models. Specifically, NeoResearch establishes an expert-inspired dual-loop research workflow, coupling hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization through experimental feedback. To enable knowledge-grounded discovery, the agent autonomously mines scientific literature from the Web, extracting modeling mechanisms, empirical evidence, and applicability conditions to formulate task-grounded, testable architecture hypotheses. Furthermore, a hierarchical experience memory links literature findings to experimental outcomes and consolidates conditional lessons, guiding architecture discovery and training optimization while supporting reuse across forecasting tasks. Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse. Our code is available.

infographic.key_insight: NeoResearch combines literature mining and experimental memory to autonomously discover lightweight, domain-specific time-series forecasting models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets reduced manual effort in forecasting architecture design and training optimization while retaining links between design choices, source evidence, and experimental outcomes.
method: Mine scientific literature for modeling mechanisms, empirical evidence, and applicability conditions.
Couple hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization in a dual-loop workflow.
Use hierarchical memory to connect literature findings with experimental outcomes and reuse conditional lessons across tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on ten datasets report competitive performance and support the dual-loop workflow, literature extraction, and memory reuse; the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Literature-derived mechanisms and reused experimental lessons require task-specific validation because their applicability depends on domain assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: NeoResearch: Literature- and Experience-Guided Autonomous Time Series Model Discovery

title: f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models
authors: Hoang Tran Vuong, Linh Ngo Van, Dang Nguyen, Thin Nguyen, Phuoc Nguyen, Mehrtash Harandi
abstract: Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types-mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model's description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model's understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of f-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated samples. DiSPaT operates through an alternating optimization: at each iteration, the current policy generates synthetic samples that serve as pseudo-anomalies, while a critic discriminator learns to distinguish these from real normal samples; this signal drives policy updates that progressively align the model distribution with the true normal-data distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors for tabular anomaly detection.

infographic.key_insight: DiSPaT uses f-divergence-based self-play to improve an LLM’s model of normal tabular data for anomaly detection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets anomaly detection in tables mixing numerical, categorical, and textual features by learning from text-serialized rows.
method: Generate synthetic rows with the current policy to serve as pseudo-anomalies.
Train a critic to distinguish generated rows from real normal rows.
Alternate critic training and policy updates to align generated and normal-data distributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors across diverse benchmarks, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Iterative generation and alternating policy–critic training may add computational cost; the abstract does not quantify this overhead.
infographic.paper_title: f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models

title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
authors: Stanislas Pamela, Nicolas Pailliez, Emmanuel Franck, Victor Michel-Dansac, Laurent Navoret, Vignesh Gopakumar
abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

infographic.key_insight: Fuse-PINN combines finite-element methods with physics-informed neural networks to enable scalable multi-GPU simulations of nonlinear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a path toward GPU-HPC simulation of challenging nonlinear physics, including fine-scale dynamics relevant to magnetic confinement fusion.
method: Formulate a mathematically grounded Finite-Element Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN).
Implement the formulation in a modular framework for GPU-based parallel computing.
Use Energy Natural Gradient Descent to support high-precision convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on fusion-relevant physics models, including nonlinear convection with fine-scale dynamics, and near-perfect multi-GPU scaling as problem size increases.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify GPU counts, absolute runtimes, or comparisons with conventional solvers, limiting assessment of practical speedups.
infographic.paper_title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs

title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
authors: Aayush Marasini, Barsat Khadka, Nick Rahimi
abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.

infographic.key_insight: WeightBench shows that frontier LLMs can interpret small neural networks and write working control policies directly in weight space, but struggle with harder model edits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Weight-space programming could enable gradient-free model inspection and modification, but current capabilities do not reliably extend to language-model patching or data-free compression.
method: Evaluate 42 tasks across weight reading, fixing, writing, impossible-edit recognition, and data-free compression.
Test networks ranging from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models.
Provide a public task registry, OS-level sandbox harness, code, and live leaderboard.
infographic.evidence_signal: Opus 5.5 scores 0.535 across all 42 tasks; on the 38-task subset evaluated for GPT-6.1-sol, GPT scores 0.568 versus Opus's 0.546.
infographic.watch_item: Agents cannot yet reliably distinguish impossible edits from difficult ones, making feasibility checks essential before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers

title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization
authors: Hiren Madhu, Sukanta Ganguly, Kiran Srinivasan, Smita Krishnaswamy, Rex Ying
abstract: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent complements the model: it reads the target database's schema and column statistics and adds validated single-row derived columns, without access to labels or model scores. On 21 RelBench tasks with leave-one-database-out pretraining on six databases, the MoREGT backbone improves on the Relational Transformer pretrained on the same databases by 2.25 points of mean AUROC and 5.83 points of mean nMAE. The agent's columns raise mean AUROC from 78.45 to 79.63 and lower mean nMAE from 27.91 to 26.98, the highest means on both metrics among the compared methods, including RT-J, which pretrains on about 400 times as many databases.

infographic.key_insight: MoREGT combines schema-routed relational experts with label-blind, agent-derived features to improve cross-database prediction using far less pretraining data than a large-corpus baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Schema-aware modeling and validated feature generation offer a practical route to transferring predictive models across platforms with different relational databases.
method: Represent rows and cells as graph-transformer tokens, adding row log-ages and foreign-key relationship names to attention.
Route row and cell tokens to experts using column metadata rather than values.
Use a label-blind LLM agent to create validated single-row derived columns from target schema and column statistics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 21 RelBench tasks with leave-one-database-out pretraining on six databases, agent features raised mean AUROC from 78.45 to 79.63 and lowered mean nMAE from 27.91 to 26.98, outperforming compared methods including RT-J, pretrained on roughly 400× as many databases.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the reported RelBench evaluation; deployment requires validating generated features and preventing label or temporal leakage.
infographic.paper_title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization

title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions
authors: Ziheng Wu, Adrian Vecina Tercero, Andre A. Fatehi, Abhik Sarkar, Brian Giera, Eric B. Duoss
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific research by integrating robotics, automated experimentation, and machine learning to execute experiments autonomously. Biology and chemistry have adopted these systems. However, increasing SDL complexity heightens susceptibility to unexpected faults in automated workflows, highlighting the need for efficient recovery mechanisms. In this study, we investigate telerobotic interventions to enhance SDL resilience against unexpected failures. We developed a teleoperation interface enabling human operators to resolve disruptions during automated tasks. The interface enables precise control of a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm (UR3e) using a 3D mouse (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro). Two velocity-based controller strategies were evaluated: (i) a coupled mode mapping all six DOFs to the 3D mouse's central knob and (ii) a decoupled mode separating translational and rotational motions. To evaluate the framework, teleoperators intervened across three SDL fault scenarios. In the first study, comparative trials showed that the decoupled controller was associated with shorter completion times and reduced rotational motion. In a second study, teleoperators performed an aiming task with and without reference-path guidance. Users were more target-driven and risk-tolerant without guidance but showed behavioral differences under different guidance strategies. These findings suggest that controller configuration and reference-path design influence operator performance during SDL fault recovery, informing teleoperation interface optimization. This work demonstrates the potential feasibility of teleoperation as a human-in-the-loop recovery mechanism for SDL workflows, combining robotic precision with human adaptability and problem-solving. These findings also provide a foundation for future studies in shared autonomy and semi-autonomous intervention.

infographic.key_insight: Human teleoperation offers a recovery mechanism for self-driving laboratories, with controller configuration and path guidance shaping operator performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adding teleoperation to autonomous lab workflows could help operators resolve unexpected faults without abandoning robotic execution.
method: Controlled a six-DOF UR3e robotic arm using a 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro.
Compared coupled six-DOF velocity control with decoupled translation and rotation.
Evaluated fault recovery and aiming behavior with and without reference-path guidance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three fault scenarios, comparative trials associated decoupled control with shorter completion times and less rotational motion; a second study found that guidance influenced aiming behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no sample sizes or quantitative effect sizes, limiting assessment of robustness and generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions

title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
authors: Thomas Brennan, Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Human-rewarded experience can teach agents task–conduct tradeoffs and increase resistance to later task-only training, though it does not guarantee violation-free behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Alignment design should account for training environments, retained experience, and deployment safeguards—not just assigned objectives.
method: Model evolutionary selection where only agents taking the rewarded action reproduce.
Compare task-only, fixed linear, and learned policies under conflicting task and conduct rewards.
Examine accumulated experience, finite memory, and hard prohibitions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical results and small-neural-network experiments illustrate how reward targets and memory affect learned tradeoffs and resistance to subsequent training.
infographic.watch_item: Violations can occur before an agent’s prevailing disposition changes; hard prohibitions may prevent them but can be costly if mispecified.
infographic.paper_title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection

title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
authors: Mohamed Aghzal, Mor Geva, Gregory J. Stein, Ziyu Yao
abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

infographic.key_insight: Mechanistic interpretability can predict and reduce web-agent hallucinations, but explaining their underlying causes remains difficult.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Probe-based steering could help prevent invalid web actions, but prompt sensitivity and disruption of valid actions limit deployment reliability.
method: Analyze Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct interacting with live websites.
Train a linear probe on last-prompt-token activations to predict hallucinations before generation.
Steer activations along the probe direction and investigate circuits underlying failures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The probe achieves 0.80 AUC, while steering corrects 85% of hallucinations but disrupts 7% of valid actions.
infographic.watch_item: A minor change in action formatting substantially weakens steering, indicating that the intervention may not generalize across prompt formats.
infographic.paper_title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination

title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
authors: Jiani Hu, Chenyan Wang, Yongkun Yang, Guanyu Hou, Jihaochen Zhang, Lei Liu
abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

infographic.key_insight: GaDiT generates disordered atomic structures and enables interpretable inverse design targeting structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate exploration of amorphous materials by linking controllable atomic disorder to desired material properties.
method: Combines a diffusion transformer with dynamic periodic graphs.
Uses masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution.
Applies conditioned atomic response mapping to identify relevant global descriptors and local atomic environments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2D amorphous carbon and 3D amorphous silicon and silica, the abstract reports high-quality generation, roughly 100× faster sampling than existing corrector-based approaches and inverse design beyond training-distribution structure–property ranges.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify validation protocols or computational costs, leaving physical reliability beyond the training distribution and practical speedups to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures

title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
authors: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo, Fangzhou Zhao, Yilong Zhao, Zekai Li
abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

infographic.key_insight: Simulation-only reinforcement learning enabled an open-weight 27B reasoning model to control real robots without demonstrations, achieving 60% success in reported real-world trials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach suggests a path to robot control through foundation-model post-training, with transfer to unseen hardware and novel instructions.
method: Build PEAR, a post-training engine for scalable simulated robot tasks.
Apply robot-use reinforcement learning on LIBERO and RoboDojo without demonstrations.
Train the model to observe, reason, and directly generate end-effector poses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported success rose from 1.6% to 74.4% on LIBERO and from 0% to 60% on a real dual-arm robot; on LIBERO-Pro task changes, the model achieved 57.4% versus 0.75% for π₀.₅.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report real-world trial counts or safety evaluations, limiting confidence in deployment reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots

title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
authors: Brandon Amos
abstract: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.

infographic.key_insight: Standard divergence computations can suffer rounding and cancellation errors when categorical distributions are nearly equal, affecting both values and gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Stable divergence calculations matter for optimization objectives in knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods.
method: Analyze numerical issues in forward and reverse KL divergence, generalized JSD, Monte Carlo KL estimates, and entropy.
Develop numerically stable reformulations with example implementations.
Validate implementations using property-based tests.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports property-based validation but provides no quantitative error reductions or downstream benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Check numerical accuracy in your target precision and autodiff framework; the abstract does not establish performance across all deployment settings.
infographic.paper_title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions

title: Sample-efficient prediction of high-entropy alloy strength through outcome-aware robust sequential learning
authors: Ahmed Shoyeb Raihan, Md Habibor Rahman, Ashish Nimbarte, Imtiaz Ahmed
abstract: Accurate prediction of high-entropy alloy (HEA) strength can guide composition and processing decisions; however, obtaining tensile-test data for HEAs can be costly and experimentally demanding. This study proposes Robust Outcome-aware Sequential Experimentation for High-Entropy Alloys (ROSE-HEA), a sample-efficient framework for predicting ultimate tensile strength (UTS) from alloy composition and processing conditions. Its acquisition policy anticipates how possible UTS outcomes update predictions and the support for complementary Gaussian process (GP) descriptions. It then reassesses the worst-case expected predictive risk remaining across a reference domain to select informative candidates. A retrospective evaluation on 501 HEA records compares ROSE-HEA with expected-improvement (EI) and upper-confidence-bound (UCB) Bayesian optimization (BO), random GP sampling, and eight conventional regressors across 30 matched runs with shared initial observations and test conditions. Starting from 25 initial observations and acquiring 100 additional responses, ROSE-HEA achieves the lowest mean root-mean-square error (RMSE), at 152.84 MPa, and the highest mean R^2, at 0.7443. Mean RMSE is reduced by 6.16% and 6.37% relative to EI and UCB, respectively. The selected observations improve prediction across six regressor families and provide broader design-space coverage. ROSE-HEA also surpasses the strongest conventional regressor's mean predictive performance using 125 rather than 185 observations, corresponding to 32.4% fewer training observations. These findings demonstrate the potential of outcome-aware robust sequential learning to improve UTS prediction in HEAs under constrained training budgets.

infographic.key_insight: ROSE-HEA improves high-entropy alloy strength prediction by selecting informative measurements through outcome-aware, robust sequential learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More sample-efficient ultimate tensile strength prediction could guide alloy composition and processing decisions while reducing costly tensile-testing needs.
method: Predict strength from alloy composition and processing using complementary Gaussian process models.
Anticipate how possible strength outcomes would update predictions and model support.
Select candidates that minimize worst-case expected predictive risk across a reference domain.
infographic.evidence_signal: In retrospective tests on 501 HEA records across 30 matched runs, ROSE-HEA reached 152.84 MPa mean RMSE and 0.7443 mean R² with 125 observations, outperforming EI and UCB and surpassing the strongest conventional regressor using 32.4% fewer training observations.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective gains require prospective experimental validation before assuming comparable savings in real alloy-development campaigns.
infographic.paper_title: Sample-efficient prediction of high-entropy alloy strength through outcome-aware robust sequential learning

title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy
authors: Miguel Tenorio, James Chapman
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.

infographic.key_insight: Local atomic-swap tests indicate that GNN feature rankings can retain physically meaningful neighbor-shell information even under deliberate overfitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Perturbation-based validation can help engineers assess whether materials-model explanations reflect local chemistry rather than compositional artifacts.
method: Deliberately overfit a physics-aware GNN ensemble to DFT-derived decomposition enthalpies for three CoMoFeNiCu stoichiometries.
Constrain output weights to encode feature importance.
Swap individual atomic sites and re-rank features to test spatial sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways, the study observed attribution changes with spatial decay consistent with the GNN interaction cutoff.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to one alloy system and three stoichiometries; generalization across chemistries remains untested.

title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders
authors: Nasir Khan, Asmaa Abdallah, Abdulkadir Celik, Ahmed M. Eltawil, Sinem Coleri, Cicek Cavdar
abstract: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. However, existing deep learning (DL)-based beam alignment methods often neglect causal relationships between inputs and outputs, resulting in limited interpretability, poor generalization, and excessive beam sweeping. Moreover, these DL solutions are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations in received power measurements can mislead beam classifiers. To overcome these issues, we propose a causally-aware DL framework integrating causal discovery into beam alignment. A two-stage causal beam selection algorithm learns a Bayesian graph capturing dependencies between received signal strength indicators (RSSI) as inputs and the optimal beam index as the target variable, then uses it to select a minimal set of relevant input features for the DL classifier. To mitigate adversarial attacks, we introduce a defensive variational autoencoder (DVAE) that maps potentially perturbed inputs back to their clean versions. End-to-end fine-tuning of the downstream beam classifier on the DVAE-reconstructed RSSI representations further boosts prediction accuracy. Simulation results show that causal beam selection achieves accuracy comparable to conventional methods while providing an \(\mathbf{829\times}\) lower per-sample computational cost than SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), a widely used explainable AI (XAI)-based feature selection method. It further reduces beam-sweeping overhead by \(\mathbf{59.4\%}\) and \(\mathbf{89.8\%}\), compared to conventional DL-based beam selection and exhaustive search, respectively. The DVAE-based defense effectively denoises adversarial inputs, sustaining 85\% accuracy across different perturbation bounds, retains baseline performance on unperturbed RSSI inputs and surpasses defensive distillation defense scheme by 15--20\% on average under different attack scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: Causal feature selection and a defensive variational autoencoder enable efficient, attack-resilient mmWave beam alignment while maintaining prediction accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce beam-training overhead and improve wireless-link resilience to manipulated received-power measurements.
method: Learn a Bayesian graph linking RSSI measurements to the optimal beam index.
Select a minimal set of relevant RSSI features for a deep-learning beam classifier.
Denoise potentially adversarial inputs with a defensive variational autoencoder and fine-tune the downstream classifier.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations report 829× lower per-sample computation than SHAP-based feature selection, 59.4% less beam-sweeping overhead than conventional DL selection, 89.8% less than exhaustive search, and 85% accuracy across tested adversarial perturbation bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation results do not establish robustness to real-world channel shifts or attacks outside the evaluated scenarios.
infographic.paper_title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders

title: ParetoM$^3$: Learning on the Pareto Set under Preference Guidance via Min-Max-Min Optimization
authors: Pei Tang, Songtao Lu
abstract: Learning across multiple inherently conflicting objectives requires selecting desirable trade-offs from the Pareto set. In this work, we study preference-guided multi-objective optimization, where a predefined preference function is minimized over the weak Pareto set of multiple nonconvex objectives. Leveraging a merit function that vanishes on the weak Pareto set, we propose a penalty-based min-max-min formulation, termed the M$^3$ problem, which unifies preference optimization and the enforcement of weak Pareto optimality in a single objective. We further develop ParetoM$^3$, a single-loop first-order algorithm for computing stationary solutions of the resulting M$^3$ problem. Under a local Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz assumption, we prove that ParetoM$^3$ finds an $ε$-stationary point of the M$^3$ problem that is also approximately weakly Pareto optimal for the original multi-objective problem when the penalty parameter is sufficiently large, with explicit non-asymptotic convergence rates. We also show that this stationarity notion recovers existing optimality criteria, including approximate preference stationarity and approximate Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, under the same assumptions used in prior works. Experiments on a synthetic benchmark, image classification, regression, and math reasoning demonstrate that ParetoM$^3$ reliably attains preferred weak Pareto optimal solutions while achieving strong practical performance. Code is available at https://github.com/tpgoodboy/ParetoM3.

infographic.key_insight: ParetoM³ combines preference optimization with weak Pareto optimality enforcement to identify desirable trade-offs among conflicting nonconvex objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a first-order approach for balancing competing model objectives according to a predefined preference function.
method: Use a merit function that vanishes on the weak Pareto set.
Combine preference minimization and a Pareto penalty in a min-max-min formulation.
Apply a single-loop first-order algorithm to seek stationary solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a synthetic benchmark, image classification, regression, and math reasoning report preferred weak Pareto solutions and strong practical performance.
infographic.watch_item: Theoretical guarantees require a local Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz assumption and a sufficiently large penalty parameter; they do not establish global preference optimality.
infographic.paper_title: ParetoM$^3$: Learning on the Pareto Set under Preference Guidance via Min-Max-Min Optimization

title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support
authors: Yifan Jin, Tao Liu
abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.

infographic.key_insight: Withholding poorly supported or high-disagreement patient simulations improves factual prediction reliability at the cost of coverage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Support and ensemble-disagreement gates offer a lightweight reliability layer for simulation-driven clinical agents, with abstention when no candidate qualifies.
method: Predict short-horizon physiological responses to norepinephrine dose categories using a recurrent dynamics ensemble.
Estimate observational action support with a behavior model and withhold simulations that fail support or disagreement thresholds.
Integrate gating into a propose–simulate–refine agent that abstains when all candidates are rejected.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used 30,700 eICU-CRD transitions across 70 hospitals, with 14 held out; at 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating achieved 7.3 mmHg MAP MAE versus 9.2 mmHg for random selection at matched coverage.
infographic.watch_item: Factual prediction accuracy and agreement with recorded actions do not establish individualized treatment effects or improved patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support

title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Tony H. Zhang, Connor Mattson, Daniel S. Brown
abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

infographic.key_insight: IBMARL bootstraps cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning from demonstrations collected one agent at a time, then learns decentralized policies that can outperform imitation alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces the need to control multiple agents simultaneously during demonstration collection and removes centralized critics at deployment.
method: Train imitation policies with Round-Robin Behavior Cloning, controlling one agent while others follow their current policies.
Use centralized critic ensembles to select among combinations of each agent’s imitation and RL action proposals.
Apply a soft Q-filtered imitation penalty only where critics prefer imitation actions; deploy RL policies alone.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four cooperative benchmarks, IBMARL surpassed its imitation policies 2.6–4.2× faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks and uniquely surpassed them on the other two; with real human demonstrations, it improved over imitation more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Selecting among joint action proposals can become costly as team size grows, and action selection depends on centralized critic accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
authors: Cole Becker, Taylan Kargin, Kimia Hassibi, Asuman Ozdaglar, Pablo A. Parrilo
abstract: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Jointly designing interpolant schedules and ODE discretizations yields condition-number-aware elliptic schedules and Zoloflow, a Gaussian sampler with minimax-optimal score-query complexity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting explicitly for target conditioning can make probability-flow sampling more efficient while providing rigorous error guarantees for Gaussian and log-concave targets.
method: Use complexified ODE trajectory analyticity to guide joint schedule and discretization design.
Derive variance-preserving schedules via conformal mapping and Jacobi elliptic functions, recovering the trigonometric schedule as κ approaches 1.
Pair elliptic schedules with a tailored discretization linked to Zolotarev optimal rational approximants.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract proves Gaussian minimax optimality among oblivious score-span algorithms and log-concave Wasserstein guarantees, and reports evaluations on synthetic and image-generation benchmarks without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Gaussian optimality assumes exact score queries; practical performance depends on score approximation quality and specifying the target condition number κ.
infographic.paper_title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond

title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
authors: Wang Ma, Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H Pham, Harsha Kokel, Qiang Ji
abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

infographic.key_insight: A black-box ensemble-of-ensembles separates prompt ambiguity from model knowledge gaps using within- and between-perturbation response variability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method enables uncertainty decomposition with sampling-only LLM access, helping engineers distinguish prompts needing clarification from answers needing verification.
method: Sample multiple responses per prompt to form an inner ensemble.
Create meaning-preserving prompt variants to form an outer ensemble.
Decompose embedding-space covariance into aleatoric and epistemic estimates, with finite-sample epistemic bias correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five short-QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, the estimator matched leading black-box methods on error ranking at a matched generation budget; paired interventions supported selective AU/EU responses, and a long-answer pilot tested claim-level factuality.
infographic.watch_item: Interpretation depends on meaning-preserving perturbations and embedding quality; the Bayesian bridge bounds a gap rather than establishing exact equivalence to Bayesian uncertainty.
infographic.paper_title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
